claim: The study used the Human Connectome Project in Aging dataset with 504 participants aged 36-100 years old.
source: using the Human Connectome Project in Aging (n=504, 36–100 years old)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the dataset used and sample characteristics in the abstract.

claim: Brain Age could uniquely add only around 1.6% in explaining variation in fluid cognition over and above chronological age.
source: Brain Age could uniquely add only around 1.6% in explaining variation in fluid cognition over and above chronological age.
evidence: This finding is based on commonality analyses reported in the results section.

claim: Better-performing age-prediction models created Brain Age that overlapped larger with chronological age, up to around 29% out of 32%, in explaining fluid cognition.
source: Instead, better-performing age-prediction models created Brain Age that overlapped larger with chronological age, up to around 29% out of 32%, in explaining fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the commonality analysis presented in the results.

claim: Brain Age missed around 11% of the total variation in fluid cognition that could have been explained by the brain variation.
source: Third, Brain Age missed around 11% of the total variation in fluid cognition that could have been explained by the brain variation.
evidence: This finding is based on comparing Brain Age with Brain Cognition in the analysis.

claim: Directly predicting fluid cognition from brain MRI data could lead to around a 1/3-time improvement of the total variation explained compared to using Brain Age and chronological age.
source: That is, directly predicting fluid cognition from brain MRI data (instead of relying on Brain Age and chronological age) could lead to around a 1/3-time improvement of the total variation explained.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between direct prediction and Brain Age-based prediction.

claim: Older adults often experience declines in several cognitive abilities such as memory, attention and processing speed, collectively known as fluid cognition.
source: Older adults often experience declines in several cognitive abilities such as memory, attention and processing speed, collectively known as fluid cognition (Salthouse, 2019; Weintraub et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Brain Age has emerged as a potential biomarker to capture fluid cognition in older adults over the past decade.
source: Over the past decade, Brain Age (Franke et al., 2010) has emerged as a potential biomarker to capture fluid cognition in older adults (Cole, 2020; Cole et al., 2018; Liem et al., 2017; Richard et al., 2018; Wrigglesworth et al., 2022; see review Boyle et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Brain Age is computed by building a prediction model that predicts chronological age based on a person's brain MRI data.
source: To compute Brain Age, researchers first build a prediction model that predicts the chronological age based on a person's brain MRI data (Baecker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citation.

claim: Brain Age is tightly close to chronological age by design.
source: Accordingly, by design, Brain Age is tightly close to chronological age.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of Brain Age.

claim: Brain Age Gap is calculated by subtracting chronological age from Brain Age.
source: Note researchers often subtract chronological age from Brain Age, creating an index known as Brain Age Gap (Franke and Gaser, 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citation.

claim: A higher value of Brain Age Gap is thought to reflect accelerated/premature aging.
source: A higher value of Brain Age Gap is thought to reflect accelerated/premature aging.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation from the literature.

claim: Brain Age Gap still depends on chronological age because it is calculated based on both Brain Age and chronological age.
source: Yet, given that Brain Age Gap is calculated based on both Brain Age and chronological age, Brain Age Gap still depends on chronological age (Butler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by citation.

claim: Brain Age demonstrates the 'regression towards the mean' phenomenon.
source: Moreover, Brain Age is known to demonstrate the 'regression towards the mean' phenomenon (Stigler, 1997).
evidence: This is a known statistical property supported by citation.

claim: Brain Age is usually shrunk towards the mean age of samples used for training the model.
source: More specifically, because Brain Age is a predicted value of a regression model that predicts chronological age, Brain Age is usually shrunk towards the mean age of samples used for training the model (Butler et al., 2021; de Lange and Cole, 2020; Le et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statistical property of regression models supported by citations.

claim: Brain Age predicts chronological age more accurately for individuals who are closer to the mean age while overestimating younger individuals' chronological age and underestimating older individuals' chronological age.
source: Accordingly, Brain Age predicts chronological age more accurately for individuals who are closer to the mean age while overestimating younger individuals' chronological age and underestimating older individuals' chronological age.
evidence: This is a consequence of regression towards the mean.

claim: There are many adjustments proposed to correct for the age dependency, but the outcomes tend to be similar to each other.
source: There are many adjustments proposed to correct for the age dependency, but the outcomes tend to be similar to each other (Beheshti et al., 2019; de Lange and Cole, 2020; Liang et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Corrected Brain Age Gap is viewed as being able to control for age dependency.
source: Corrected Brain Age Gap in particular is viewed as being able to control for age dependency (Butler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The improvement in predicting chronological age may not necessarily make Brain Age Gap better at capturing fluid cognition.
source: However, the improvement in predicting chronological age may not necessarily make Brain Age Gap better at capturing fluid cognition (Jirsaraie et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is a finding from cited literature.

claim: If the age-prediction model had perfect performance, Brain Age Gap would be exactly zero and would have no utility in capturing fluid cognition beyond chronological age.
source: If, for instance, the age-prediction model had the perfect performance, Brain Age Gap would be exactly zero and would have no utility in capturing fluid cognition beyond chronological age.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of perfect prediction.

claim: Previous studies found reasonable predictive performances of cognition-prediction models built from certain MRI modalities.
source: Previous studies found reasonable predictive performances of these cognition-prediction models, built from certain MRI modalities (Dubois et al., 2018; Pat et al., 2022; Rasero et al., 2021; Sripada et al., 2020; Tetereva et al., 2022; for review, see Vieira et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The variation in fluid cognition explained by Brain Cognition should be higher or equal to that explained by Brain Age by design.
source: This is, by design, the variation in fluid cognition explained by Brain Cognition should be higher or equal to that explained by Brain Age.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the design of the study.

claim: The study built 26 age-prediction models for Brain Age based on different combinations of MRI modalities.
source: we built 26 age-prediction models for Brain Age based on different combinations of MRI modalities, using the Human Connectome Project in Aging (n=504, 36–100 years old).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the study design.

claim: There is a negative relationship between chronological age and fluid cognition (r(502) = –0.57, p<0.001, R2=0.32).
source: Figure 1a shows the negative relationship between chronological age and fluid cognition (r(502) = –0.57, p<0.001, R2=0.32).
evidence: This is a statistical finding presented in the results with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Older individuals tended to have a lower fluid cognition score.
source: Older individuals tended to have a lower fluid cognition score.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative correlation between age and fluid cognition.

claim: The top-four age-prediction models that performed similarly were 'stacked' models that included multiple sets of brain MRI features with R2 >0.76, r>0.83, MAE <65 months.
source: For age prediction, the top-four models that performed similarly were 'stacked' models that included multiple sets of brain MRI features: 'Stacked: All excluding Task Contrast', 'Non Task', 'All excluding Task FC' and 'All' (R2 >0.76, r>0.83, MAE <65 months).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the predictive modeling analysis.

claim: For fluid cognition prediction, the top-performing model was 'Stacked: All' (R2=0.393, r=0.627, MAE = 7.7 points).
source: For fluid cognition prediction, the top-performing model was 'Stacked: All' (R2=0.393, r=0.627, MAE = 7.7 points).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the predictive modeling analysis.

claim: The best set of features across age and fluid cognition prediction was cortical thickness.
source: The best set of features across age and fluid cognition prediction was cortical thickness.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the predictive modeling analysis.

claim: Across sets of MRI features, the age-prediction models tended to provide higher R2 and r than the fluid cognition-prediction models.
source: Across sets of MRI features, the age-prediction models tended to provide higher R2 and r than the fluid cognition-prediction models.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the predictive modeling analysis.

claim: Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age created from higher-performing age-prediction models explained a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
source: Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age created from higher-performing age-prediction models explained a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a finding from the simple regression analysis.

claim: Brain Age Gap created from lower-performing age-prediction models explained a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
source: However, Brain Age Gap created from the lower-performing age-prediction models explained a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a finding from the simple regression analysis.

claim: The top performing age-prediction model, 'Stacked: All excluding Task Contrast', generated Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age that explained the highest amount of variation in fluid cognition, but produced Brain Age Gap that explained the least amount of variation in fluid cognition.
source: For instance, the top performing age-prediction model, 'Stacked: All excluding Task Contrast', generated Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age that explained the highest amount of variation in fluid cognition, but, at the same time, produced Brain Age Gap that explained the least amount of variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a specific example from the simple regression analysis.

claim: The amount of variation in fluid cognition explained by Corrected Brain Age Gap was relatively small (maximum at R2=0.041) across age-prediction models and did not relate to the predictive performance of the age-prediction models.
source: On the contrary, an amount of variation in fluid cognition explained by Corrected Brain Age Gap was relatively small (maximum at R2=0.041) across age-prediction models and did not relate to the predictive performance of the age-prediction models.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simple regression analysis.

claim: Brain Cognition appeared to explain a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition than any Brain Age indices, especially for top-performing age/cognition-prediction models.
source: Brain Cognition appeared to explain a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition than any Brain Age indices, especially for top-performing age/cognition-prediction models (e.g. Stacked: All).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the simple regression analysis with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: R2 for multiple regression models having both chronological age and each Brain Age index as regressors was M=0.326 (SD = 0.005).
source: We found R2 for these models at M=0.326 (SD = 0.005).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the multiple regression analysis.

claim: The unique effects of Brain Age indices were all relatively small (maximum at ΔR2Brain Age index = 0.0161, with statistically significant at p-value <0.05 in 10 out of 26 models) across the four Brain Age indices and across different age-prediction models.
source: The unique effects of Brain Age indices were all relatively small (maximum at ΔR2Brain Age index = 0.0161, with statistically significant at p-value <0.05 in 10 out of 26 models) across the four Brain Age indices and across different age-prediction models.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: Different Brain Age indices led to different levels of the unique effects of chronological age and the common effects between chronological age and Brain Age indices.
source: However, it is clear that different Brain Age indices led to different levels of the unique effects of chronological age and the common effects between chronological age and Brain Age indices.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: For the top-performing age-prediction models, the unique effects of chronological age were low for Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age, but high for Brain Age Gap.
source: For the top-performing age-prediction models (e.g. Stacked: All excluding Task Contrast), the unique effects of chronological age were low for Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age, but high for Brain Age Gap.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: The lower-performing age-prediction models provided high common effects for Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age, but low for Brain Age Gap.
source: On the contrary, the lower-performing age-prediction models provided high common effects for Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age, but low for Brain Age Gap.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: For Corrected Brain Age Gap, the unique effects of chronological age were much higher than the common effects across all age-prediction models.
source: Nonetheless, for Corrected Brain Age Gap, the unique effects of chronological age were much higher than the common effects across all age-prediction models.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: R2 for multiple regression models having chronological age, each Brain Age index and Brain Cognition as regressors was M=0.385 (SD = 0.042).
source: We found R2 for these models at M=0.385 (SD = 0.042).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the multiple regression analysis.

claim: The unique effects of Brain Cognition appeared much larger (maximum at ΔR2cognition = 0.1183, statistically significant p-value at 0.05 in 24 out of 26 models).
source: On the contrary, the unique effects of Brain Cognition appeared much larger (maximum at ΔR2cognition = 0.1183, statistically significant p-value at 0.05 in 24 out of 26 models).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: For top-performing age/cognition-prediction models, the largest proportion of fluid cognition was attributed to (a) the common effects among the three for Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age and (b) the common effects between chronological age and Brain Cognition for Brain Age Gap and Corrected Brain Age Gap.
source: For top-performing age/cognition-prediction models (e.g. Stacked All), the largest proportion of fluid cognition was attributed to (a) the common effects among the three for Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age and (b) the common effects between chronological age and Brain Cognition for Brain Age Gap and Corrected Brain Age Gap.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: Brain Age itself did not add much more information to help capture fluid cognition than what was already known from a person's chronological age.
source: First, Brain Age itself did not add much more information to help us capture fluid cognition than what we had already known from a person's chronological age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the commonality analysis results.

claim: Without Brain Age indices, chronological age by itself already explained around 32% of the variation in fluid cognition.
source: Without Brain Age indices, chronological age by itself already explained around 32% of the variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the regression analysis.

claim: Including Brain Age indices only added around 1.6% at best to the variation in fluid cognition explained.
source: Including Brain Age indices only added around 1.6% at best.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: The small unique effects of Brain Age were inevitable because, by design, Brain Age is tightly close to chronological age.
source: We believe the small unique effects of Brain Age were inevitable because, by design, Brain Age is tightly close to chronological age.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the design of Brain Age.

claim: Chronological age and Brain Age captured mostly a similar variation in fluid cognition.
source: Therefore, chronological age and Brain Age captured mostly a similar variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is an inference from the commonality analysis results.

claim: Higher-performing age-prediction models created Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age that captured a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
source: In the simple regression models, higher-performing age-prediction models, such as stacked models, created Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age that captured a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a finding from the simple regression analysis.

claim: Both Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age from higher-performing age-prediction models were closer to the real chronological age of participants.
source: Because both Brain Age and Corrected Brain Age from higher-performing age-prediction models were closer to the real chronological age of participants, their ability to capture fluid cognition mirrored the ability of chronological age.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between prediction performance and explanatory power.

claim: The commonality analysis showed higher common effects between (Corrected) Brain Age and chronological age from higher-performing age-prediction models.
source: The commonality analysis confirmed this by showing higher common effects between (Corrected) Brain Age and chronological age from higher-performing age-prediction models.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: Lower-performing age-prediction models created Brain Age Gap that explained a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
source: In contrast, lower-performing (as opposed to higher-performing) age-prediction models, such as CARIT NoGo-Go, created Brain Age Gap that explained a higher amount of variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a finding from the simple regression analysis.

claim: When Brain Age was a poor indicator of the real chronological age, the utility of Brain Age Gap is driven more by the real chronological age.
source: And when Brain Age was a poor indicator of the real chronological age, the utility of Brain Age Gap is driven more by the real chronological age (Butler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Corrected Brain Age Gap showed weak effects on the simple regression models across all age-prediction models (max at around 4.1% of variation explained).
source: Corrected Brain Age Gap, on the other hand, showed weak effects on the simple regression models across all age-prediction models (max at around 4.1% of variation explained).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simple regression analysis.

claim: Corrected Brain Age Gap was the only index among the four that appeared to deconfound the influences of chronological age on the relationship between brain aging and fluid cognition.
source: Corrected Brain Age Gap was the only index among the four that appeared to deconfound the influences of chronological age on the relationship between brain aging and fluid cognition (Butler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a claim about the properties of Corrected Brain Age Gap supported by citation.

claim: The common effects between Corrected Brain Age Gap and chronological age were small but most were not zero (max at around 3.3% of variation explained).
source: Note while these common effects between Corrected Brain Age Gap and chronological age were small, most were not zero (max at around 3.3% of variation explained).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: The correction done to deconfound the influences of chronological age on Corrected Brain Age Gap may not be perfect.
source: This means that the correction done to deconfound the influences of chronological age on Corrected Brain Age Gap (de Lange and Cole, 2020) may not be perfect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that common effects were not zero.

claim: The estimation of the influences of chronological age was done in the training set, which might not fully be applicable to the test sets.
source: Perhaps this is because the estimation of the influences of chronological age was done in the training set, which might not fully be applicable to the test sets.
evidence: This is a speculation about why the correction may not be perfect.

claim: After controlling for the influences of chronological age, Corrected Brain Age Gap could only account for a small amount of variation in fluid cognition.
source: Still, weak effects of Corrected Brain Age Gap in the simple regression indicate that, after controlling for the influences of chronological age, this Brain Age index could only account for a small amount of variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simple regression results.

claim: The small effects of the Corrected Brain Age Gap in explaining fluid cognition of aging individuals found here are consistent with studies in older adults and younger populations.
source: The small effects of the Corrected Brain Age Gap in explaining fluid cognition of aging individuals found here are consistent with studies in older adults (Cole, 2020) and younger populations (Butler et al., 2021; Jirsaraie et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from cited literature.

claim: Cole, 2020 studied the utility of Brain Age on cognitive functioning of large samples (n>17,000) of older adults, aged 45–80 years, from the UK Biobank.
source: Cole, 2020 studied the utility of Brain Age on cognitive functioning of large samples (n>17,000) of older adults, aged 45–80 years, from the UK Biobank (Sudlow et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of a cited study.

claim: Cole, 2020 found Corrected Brain Age Gap to be significantly related to performance in four out of six cognitive measures, with small effect sizes (maximum partial eta-squared at .0059).
source: He found Corrected Brain Age Gap to be significantly related to performance in four out of six cognitive measures, and among those significant relationships, the effect sizes were small with a maximum of partial eta-squared at.0059.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Jirsaraie et al., 2023a studied the utility of Brain Age on cognitive functioning of youths aged 8–22 years old from the Human Connectome Project in Development and Preschool Depression Study.
source: Similarly, Jirsaraie et al., 2023a studied the utility of Brain Age on cognitive functioning of youths aged 8–22 years old from the Human Connectome Project in Development (Somerville et al., 2018) and Preschool Depression Study (Luby, 2010).
evidence: This is a description of a cited study.

claim: Jirsaraie et al., 2023b found weak effects of the adjusted Brain Age Gap on cognitive functioning across five cognitive tasks, five age-prediction models and two datasets (mean of standardised regression coefficient = –0.09).
source: Using multiple regressions, Jirsaraie et al., 2023b found weak effects of the adjusted Brain Age Gap on cognitive functioning across five cognitive tasks, five age-prediction models and the two datasets (mean of standardised regression coefficient = –0.09, see their Table S7).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Butler et al., 2021 studied the utility of Brain Age on cognitive functioning of youths aged 8–22 years old from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort.
source: Next, Butler et al., 2021 studied the utility of Brain Age on cognitive functioning of another group of youths aged 8–22 years old from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC) (Satterthwaite et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of a cited study.

claim: Butler et al., 2021 found a weak, statistically non-significant correlation between the adjusted Brain Age Gap and cognitive functioning at r=-0.01, p=0.71.
source: Similar to the aforementioned results, Butler et al., 2021 found a weak, statistically non-significant correlation between the adjusted Brain Age Gap and cognitive functioning at r=-0.01, p=0.71.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: The utility of Brain Age in explaining cognitive functioning beyond chronological age appears to be weak across age groups, different predictive modelling algorithms and age-dependency adjustments.
source: Accordingly, the utility of Brain Age in explaining cognitive functioning beyond chronological age appears to be weak across age groups, different predictive modelling algorithms and age-dependency adjustments.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The predictive performance of age-prediction models did not correspond to the utility of Brain Age in capturing fluid cognition over and above chronological age.
source: Second, the predictive performance of age-prediction models did not correspond to the utility of Brain Age in capturing fluid cognition over and above chronological age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of multiple regression models.

claim: The best-performing age-prediction model was 'Stacked: All excluding Task Contrast' (R2=0.775), but the unique effects of Brain Age indices from this model were weak (ΔR2Brain Age index ≤0.0048) and not statistically significant.
source: For instance, while the best-performing age-prediction model was 'Stacked: All excluding Task Contrast' (R2=0.775), the unique effects of Brain Age indices from this model in the two-regressor multiple regressions (i.e. with a Brain Age index and chronological age as regressor) were weak (ΔR2Brain Age index ≤0.0048) and not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a specific example from the analysis.

claim: The highest unique effects of Brain Age indices in the two-regressor multiple regression models were from the FACENAME: Distractor model (ΔR2Brain Age index ≤0.0135, p<0.05) that had a poorer performance in predicting chronological age (R2=0.204).
source: The highest unique effects of Brain Age indices in the two-regressor multiple regression models were from the FACENAME: Distractor model (ΔR2Brain Age index ≤0.0135, p<0.05) that had a poorer performance in predicting chronological age (R2=0.204).
evidence: This is a specific example from the analysis.

claim: A race to improve the performance of age-prediction models does not necessarily enhance the utility of Brain Age indices as a biomarker for fluid cognition.
source: Accordingly, a race to improve the performance of age-prediction models (Baecker et al., 2021) does not necessarily enhance the utility of Brain Age indices as a biomarker for fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: The discrepancy between the predictive performance of age-prediction models and the utility of Brain Age indices as a biomarker is consistent with recent findings in the context of cognitive functioning and neurological/psychological disorders.
source: This discrepancy between the predictive performance of age-prediction models and the utility of Brain Age indices as a biomarker is consistent with recent findings (for review, see Jirsaraie et al., 2023a), both in the context of cognitive functioning (Jirsaraie et al., 2023b) and neurological/psychological disorders (Bashyam et al., 2020; Rokicki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from cited literature.

claim: Combining different MRI modalities into the prediction models often leads to the highest performance of age-prediction models, but does not likely explain the highest variance across different phenotypes.
source: For instance, combining different MRI modalities into the prediction models, similar to our stacked models, often leads to the highest performance of age-prediction models, but does not likely explain the highest variance across different phenotypes, including cognitive functioning and beyond (Jirsaraie et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Brain Cognition allowed the study to gauge the variation in fluid cognition that is related to the brain MRI, and thereby, to estimate the upper limit of what Brain Age can do.
source: More specifically, using Brain Cognition allowed us to gauge the variation in fluid cognition that is related to the brain MRI, and thereby, to estimate the upper limit of what Brain Age can do.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological approach.

claim: By examining what was captured by Brain Cognition over and above Brain Age and chronological age, the study was able to quantify the amount of co-variation between brain MRI and fluid cognition that was missed by Brain Age.
source: Moreover, by examining what was captured by Brain Cognition, over and above Brain Age and chronological age via the unique effects of Brain Cognition, we were able to quantify the amount of co-variation between brain MRI and fluid cognition that was missed by Brain Age.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological approach.

claim: Brain Cognition, especially from certain cognition-prediction models such as the stacked models, has relatively good predictive performance.
source: From our results, Brain Cognition, especially from certain cognition-prediction models such as the stacked models, has relatively good predictive performance, consistent with previous studies (Dubois et al., 2018; Pat et al., 2022; Rasero et al., 2021; Sripada et al., 2020; Tetereva et al., 2022; for review, see Vieira et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis compared with cited literature.

claim: Brain Cognition exhibited large common effects with chronological age.
source: Similar to Brain Age indices, Brain Cognition exhibited large common effects with chronological age.
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: Unlike Brain Age indices, Brain Cognition showed large unique effects, up to around 11%.
source: But more importantly, unlike Brain Age indices, Brain Cognition showed large unique effects, up to around 11%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: The unique effects of Brain Cognition indicated the amount of co-variation between brain MRI and fluid cognition that was missed by a Brain Age index and chronological age.
source: As explained above, the unique effects of Brain Cognition indicated the amount of co-variation between brain MRI and fluid cognition that was missed by a Brain Age index and chronological age.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the unique effects of Brain Cognition.

claim: The missing amount of variation explained by Brain Cognition was relatively high, considering that Brain Age and chronological age together explained around 32% of the total variation in fluid cognition.
source: This missing amount was relatively high, considering that Brain Age and chronological age together explained around 32% of the total variation in fluid cognition.
evidence: This is a comparative interpretation of the findings.

claim: If a Brain Age index was used as a biomarker along with chronological age, researchers would have missed an opportunity to improve the performance of the model by around one-third of the variation explained.
source: Accordingly, if a Brain Age index was used as a biomarker along with chronological age, we would have missed an opportunity to improve the performance of the model by around one-third of the variation explained.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Brain Age and Brain Cognition.

claim: HCP-A used state-of-the-art MRI methodologies.
source: While HCP-A used state-of-the-art MRI methodologies, covered a wide age range from 36 to 100 years old and used several task-fMRI from different tasks that are harder to find in other bigger databases (e.g. UK Biobank from Sudlow et al., 2015), several characteristics of HCP-A might limit the generalisability of our findings.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset characteristics.

claim: The tasks used in task-based fMRI in HCP-A are not used widely in clinical settings.
source: For instance, the tasks used in task-based fMRI in HCP-A are not used widely in clinical settings (Horien et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a limitation noted with citation.

claim: HCP-A excluded participants with neurological conditions, possibly making their participants not representative of the general population.
source: Similarly, HCP-A also excluded participants with neurological conditions, possibly making their participants not representative of the general population.
evidence: This is a limitation of the dataset.

claim: HCP-A does not include younger populations.
source: Similarly, HCP-A does not include younger populations.
evidence: This is a limitation of the dataset.

claim: There is a notable difference between studies investigating the utility of Brain Age in explaining cognitive functioning and those explaining neurological/psychological disorders.
source: There is a notable difference between studies investigating the utility of Brain Age in explaining cognitive functioning, including ours and others (e.g. Butler et al., 2021; Cole, 2020; Cole, 2020; Jirsaraie et al., 2023b) and those explaining neurological/psychological disorders (e.g. Bashyam et al., 2020; Rokicki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison between different types of studies.

claim: Normative studies focus on largely healthy participants, while case-control studies compare participants without vs. with neurological/psychological disorders.
source: We consider the former as a normative type of study and the latter as a case-control type of study (Insel et al., 2010; Marquand et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a categorization of study types with citations.

claim: Case-control studies treat Brain Age as a method to detect anomalies in the neurological/psychological group.
source: On the one hand, this means that case-control studies treat Brain Age as a method to detect anomalies in the neurological/psychological group (Hahn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of how case-control studies use Brain Age, supported by citation.

claim: Case-control studies have to ignore under-fitted models when applied prediction models built from largely healthy participants to participants with neurological/psychological disorders.
source: On the other hand, this also means that case-control studies have to ignore under-fitted models when applied prediction models built from largely healthy participants to participants with neurological/psychological disorders (i.e. Brain Age may predict chronological age well for the controls, but not for those with a disorder).
evidence: This is a limitation of case-control studies.

claim: The age-prediction models for explaining cognitive functioning in normative studies do not suffer from being under-fitted.
source: Accordingly, the age-prediction models for explaining cognitive functioning in normative studies, while not allowing us to detect group-level anomalies, do not suffer from being under-fitted.

claim: The generalisability of the study might be limited to just the normative type of study.
source: This unfortunately might limit the generalisability of our study into just the normative type of study.

claim: Future work is needed to test the utility of brain age in the case-control case.
source: Future work is still needed to test the utility of brain age in the case-control case.

claim: Researchers should be aware of the overlap in variation between Brain Age and chronological age and should focus on the contribution of Brain Age over and above chronological age.
source: First, they have to be aware of the overlap in variation between Brain Age and chronological age and should focus on the contribution of Brain Age over and above chronological age.

claim: Using Brain Age Gap will not fix the overlap between Brain Age and chronological age.
source: Using Brain Age Gap will not fix this.

claim: It is critical that readers of past literature note whether or not age was controlled for when testing for effects on the Brain Age Gap.
source: Butler et al., 2021 recently highlighted this point, "These results indicate that the association between cognition and the BAG [Brain Age Gap] are driven by the association between age and cognitive performance. As such, it is critical that readers of past literature note whether or not age was controlled for when testing for effects on the BAG, as this has not always been common practice (p. 4097)."
evidence: This is a recommendation from cited literature.

claim: Future work should account for the relationship between Brain Age and chronological age, either using Corrected Brain Age Gap or examining unique effects of Brain Age indices after controlling for chronological age through commonality analyses.
source: Similar to previous recommendations (Butler et al., 2021; Le et al., 2018), we suggest future work should account for the relationship between Brain Age and chronological age, either using Corrected Brain Age Gap (or other similar adjustments) or, better, examining unique effects of Brain Age indices after controlling for chronological age through commonality analyses.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings and previous literature.

claim: The authors prefer using the commonality analysis as it can decompose variance of the phenotype of interest into unique and common effects.
source: Note we prefer using the commonality analysis as it can decompose variance of the phenotype of interest into unique and common effects, allowing us to understand the shared variance between chronological age and Brain Age indices (Ray‐Mukherjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological preference with citation.

claim: Brain Age indices had the same unique effects regardless of the level of common effects they had with chronological age.
source: In our case, Brain Age indices had the same unique effects regardless of the level of common effects they had with chronological age (e.g. Brain Age vs. Corrected Brain Age Gap from stacked models).
evidence: This is a finding from the commonality analysis.

claim: In the case of fluid cognition, the unique effects of Brain Age might be too small to be clinically meaningful.
source: In the case of fluid cognition, the unique effects might be too small to be clinically meaningful as shown here and previously (Butler et al., 2021; Cole, 2020; Jirsaraie et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study findings and cited literature.

claim: Researchers should not select age-prediction models based solely on age-prediction performance.

claim: Researchers could select age-prediction models that explained phenotypes of interest the best.

claim: Selecting age-prediction models based on a set of features was found effective not only for fluid cognition but also for neurological and psychological disorders.
source: Here, we selected age-prediction models based on a set of features (i.e., modalities) of brain MRI. This strategy was found effective not only for fluid cognition as we demonstrated here, but also for neurological and psychological disorders as shown elsewhere (Jirsaraie et al., 2023a; Rokicki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the study and cited literature.

source: Rokicki et al., 2021, for instance, found that, while integrating across MRI modalities led to age-prediction models with the highest age-prediction performance, using only T1 structural MRI gave age-prediction models that were better at classifying Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Using only cerebral blood flow gave age-prediction models that were better at classifying mild/subjective cognitive impairment, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
source: Similarly, using only cerebral blood flow gave age-prediction models that were better at classifying mild/subjective cognitive impairment, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Jirsaraie et al., 2023a compared gradient tree boosting (GTB) and deep-learning brain network (DBN) algorithms in building age-prediction models and found GTB to have higher age-prediction performance but DBN to have better utility in explaining cognitive functioning.
source: For instance, Jirsaraie et al., 2023a compared gradient tree boosting (GTB) and deep-learning brain network (DBN) algorithms in building age-prediction models. They found GTB to have higher age-prediction performance but DBN to have better utility in explaining cognitive functioning.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: An algorithm with better utility should be used for explaining a phenotype of interest.
source: In this case, an algorithm with better utility (e.g. DBN) should be used for explaining a phenotype of interest.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on cited findings.

claim: Bashyam et al., 2020 found that DBN-based age-prediction models with a moderate number of epochs were better at classifying Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment and schizophrenia than those with higher or lower number of epochs.
source: Bashyam et al., 2020 made a similar observation, though for a contradictory conclusion, see Hahn et al., 2021. Bashyam and colleagues built different DBN-based age-prediction models, varying in age-prediction performance. The DBN models with a higher number of epochs corresponded to higher age-prediction performance. However, DBN-based age-prediction models with a moderate (as opposed to higher or lower) number of epochs were better at classifying Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment and schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: There is a persisting assumption across several studies that the most accurate brain age models will have the most potential for detecting differences in a given phenotype of interest.
source: In any case, this calls for a change in research practice, as recently pointed out by Jirsaraie et al., 2023a, "Despite mounting evidence, there is a persisting assumption across several studies that the most accurate brain age models will have the most potential for detecting differences in a given phenotype of interest".
evidence: This is a quote from cited literature.

claim: Future neuroimaging research should aim to build age-prediction models that are not necessarily good at predicting age, but at capturing phenotypes of interest.
source: Future neuroimaging research should aim to build age-prediction models that are not necessarily good at predicting age, but at capturing phenotypes of interest.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Researchers should test how much Brain Age miss the variation in the brain MRI that could explain fluid cognition or other phenotypes of interest.

source: As demonstrated here, one straightforward method is to build a prediction model using a phenotype of interest as the target (e.g. fluid cognition) and incorporate the predicted value of this model (e.g. Brain Cognition), along with Brain Age and chronological age, into a multiple regression for commonality analyses.

claim: Brain Age missed up to around one-third of the variation in fluid cognition that could have been explained by brain MRI.
source: Third, Brain Age missed up to around one-third of the variation in fluid cognition that could have been explained by brain MRI.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Future empirical research is needed to test the utility of Brain Age on other phenotypes, especially when Brain Age is used for anomaly detection in case-control studies.
source: Yet, given our focus on fluid cognition, future empirical research is needed to test the utility of Brain Age on other phenotypes, especially when Brain Age is used for anomaly detection in case-control studies (e.g. Bashyam et al., 2020; Rokicki et al., 2021).
